questions.q: According to this lesson, why doesn't adding a second cloud provider double the security workload?
options: AWS and Azure share the exact same console and APIs
The underlying security primitives (identity, policy enforcement, logging, threat detection) are the same across clouds — only the product names and syntax differ
A second cloud provider never needs its own security controls
CIS Benchmarks only cover one cloud provider at a time, so the other can be ignored
questions.explain: The hard part of cloud security is understanding primitives like identity and policy enforcement, which are conceptually identical across clouds — adding AWS is largely translation, not re-learning from zero.

questions.q: Which pairing correctly matches an Azure security primitive to its AWS equivalent as described in this lesson?
options: Microsoft Entra ID maps to AWS IAM / IAM Identity Center
Azure Policy maps to Amazon GuardDuty
Microsoft Defender for Cloud maps to AWS CloudTrail
Azure Monitor maps to AWS Organizations
questions.explain: Entra ID is Azure's identity provider; AWS IAM and IAM Identity Center serve the equivalent identity function on AWS.

questions.q: Where does this lesson say the genuine extra effort of dual-cloud security actually goes?
options: Nowhere — there is zero additional work from adding a second cloud
Rewriting the entire security program from scratch for each cloud
Memorizing a completely unrelated set of security concepts for AWS
Terminology/scope translation, federated identity management, log aggregation, and mapping one control framework onto two native toolsets
questions.explain: The real costs are translating boundary concepts (e.g., resource group vs. account), federating identity to one source of truth, aggregating logs/alerts, and implementing one framework's intent across two sets of native tools.

questions.q: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP) in AWS, as described in this lesson?
options: A per-instance firewall rule identical to a Network Security Group
A billing report generated monthly by AWS Cost Explorer
An AWS Organizations guardrail that sets maximum permissions across accounts in an OU, conceptually parallel to Azure Policy at the management-group level
A replacement for IAM that eliminates the need for identity policies
questions.explain: SCPs act as organization-wide guardrails on allowed permissions, serving a similar role to Azure Policy applied at the management-group level.

questions.q: What does it mean that Microsoft Defender for Cloud now supports AWS as a first-class environment, per this lesson?
options: Connecting an AWS account surfaces its CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark findings, GuardDuty alerts, and Security Hub findings in the same secure score and recommendations view used for Azure
Defender for Cloud replaces the need for AWS IAM entirely
AWS security findings must still be reviewed in a completely separate console with no overlap
Defender for Cloud can only monitor Azure resources and treats AWS as read-only metadata
questions.explain: Defender for Cloud ingests AWS-native findings (CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark, GuardDuty, Security Hub) into the same unified secure score and recommendations experience used for Azure, which is the practical convergence point the lesson describes.
